speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Alphonse
Fournier for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cold well.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to prolong this debate unduly, because I think it has perhaps gone too long already. I was astonished to learn t-hait I am the 136th speaker, and I am included in the previous 135. I was astonished also to learn that of the 135 who have spoken, 95 are supporters of my right hon. friend, including, if I may say so, the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) who has constituted himself a party sole in this house. My primary object in asking your indulgence and the indulgence of hon. members is to pay at least some attention to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I desire to analyse his position, although not at great length, and compare his amendment with my own. I shall make other observations, some of which may not be strictly in order. If they are not, then I ask the indulgence of this house. During the course of my remarks, I desire to say something about the victory loan now before the country and to give it my support. I do not intend to proceed precisely in the order I have indicated.
Before going any further, I should like to offer to my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty), who is just departing from the chamber, my congratulations upon his natal day and upon being fifty-three years young. On coming into this house after an absence of five years I found him occupying a most responsible position in the government of this country. He has been universally courteous to me and I appreciate it. With these few brief preliminary observations, may I refer to the course of the debate.
Although I consider the debate has been long, I consider also that for the most part it has been conducted upon a very high plane. Of course, there have been a few glaring exceptions, but on the whole I think I am justified, notwithstanding any criticism that may have been levelled at the debate from outside the house, in saying that I believe most hon. gentlemen have shown a sense of their responsibility, having regard to the distressing times through which we, in common with our allies, are now passing. So far as I am concerned personally I have tried at all times to keep the debate on a high plane and to avoid raising strife, especially racial strife. I do not think anyone can accuse me of doing that here in the past, nor will they
6S8	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
be able to accuse me of doing it in the future. In any appeal I have made in this house or in the country I have tried to appeal to reason alone, and I shall continue to pursue that course no matter what criticism I receive.
Aside altogether from the speeches of cabinet ministers who have participated in this debate, there have been two or three others that are outstanding. I should like to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray) upon the manner and matter of the speech he made. I think it took great courage on the part of the hon. gentleman to say what he did. The plane upon which he carried on his discussion was of the highest, and I think it was one of the best speeches we have heard in this house.
I should like to offer a token of appreciation to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore), who I am sorry is not in his seat at the moment, for his address. It revealed to me an intelligent grasp of the problem of government which I do not think is excelled and perhaps not even equalled by any other member of the house.
I am sorry to say that there have been other speeches delivered during the course of this debate which do not deserve such praise as I have attempted to shower upon the two members to whom I have referred. I listened with the greatest regret, and as intently as I possibly could, to the speech of my fellow New Brunswicker, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), and in my view it was one of the most dangerous speeches ever uttered in this House of Commons during all the years I have been here. I say, further, that I think it was quite unworthy of the hon. member and, from his own personal position, quite unnecessary. The particular part of his speech to which I refer was that portion in which he declared that the issue of compulsory military service was a racial issue. I deny that allegation categorically and with all the force and power at my command. I do suggest that there is no racial issue involved.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You made it one in 1917.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was no racial issue involved in this question, now or then or at any other time. It has become a political issue, and for that I am truly sorry. There is raised in this issue only the question of equality of service and equality of sacrifice. The hon. member for Gloucester has made a speech which is designed to set race against race; and having regard to the conditions existing in the province of New Brunswick from which we both come, it may have reper-

cussions which will not help the position of those whom he champions.
I deplore the attitude of the hon. member for Gloucester. He knows, as I do, that the Acadian portion of our people is loyal. I have said so before, and I reaffirm it now, that it has enlisted for active service in far greater numbers than it did in the last war; that as opportunity offered, men came to the colours- an opportunity which was denied them in the early stages of the war by the ineptitude of the recruiting officials of the Department of National Defence, a situation which was rectified after proper representations were made to them. I understand from officers in the army that these young men have made good soldiers. I saw many of them in Britain and I am glad to pay this tribute to them.
One of the difficulties with respect to our young Acadian men in New Brunswick was that in the early stages of the war there was a lack of trained officers and instructors speaking the French language, but that difficulty has, I believe, been overcome in very large degree. I verily believe, and I want to pay this compliment to our Acadian population, that they would have accepted compulsory service without any demur if their leaders, including the hon. member for Gloucester, had shown the way. On the contrary, he has indicated his determination to make this not only a political but a racial issue. I deplore that. How can his action help the cause of national unity? I am going to leave his speech there.

speechtext:
I am
thankful for that information, and if I can get around to reading it within the next two or three years, I shall probably do so.
While we have been debating the issues raised in this debate, what has been happening outside? With the exception of the position in Russia, the campaign in every other theatre of war has been going froAi bad to worse. Never since Dunkirk have I felt so upset as I was on Sunday with the fall of the great 'bastion of Singapore, announced by Mr. Churchill. The position in the Pacific has been one of continued deterioration. No wonder that Australia is alarmed!
Then there was the spectacle of the German warships successfully negotiating the strait of Dover in the face of the combined resources of the British air and naval forces-something which had never been accomplished by a foe of Britain in more than a century.
These are things to make one think, and certainly I drew some conclusions. One of them was this. If we do not face realities, we may lose this war. We have a just cause, and the intentions of all of us, this government included, are of the very best. But we cannot win this war with good intentions, even if we have a just cause.
Canada's war effort has passed the organization stage and we are now in production. Great strides have been made; let us freely admit that. But because great strides, on a comparative basis, have been made, do not let us be lulled into a sense of false security. That I fear is happening here. That I fear is happening in the United States, judging by the newspaper reports to-day. That has happened all along in Canada. It is not enough for ministers to make laudatory speeches so long as there remains so much to be done, so long as our position in this struggle is at such a low ebb. I am speaking of the whole picture-not of just our own effort.
Let me illustrate. A few days ago Mr. Ralph Bell, for whom I have a very high regard, told the board of trade in an eastern city that the growth of aircraft production in Canada had been eighty per cent, and he added that it had been "one of the industrial romances of the British empire." That is very fine stuff for an after-dinner speech, but what in fact does it mean? Eighty per cent of what? It really -means nothing in- terms of production. What was our production of planes? Practically nothing before this war-thirty planes a year. It is just that sort of extravagant statement which breeds complacency.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, he spoke of ministerial statements. Mr. Bell was not speaking for the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He was, as a matter of fact, speaking contrary to instructions issued to all officers of the department.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Does that apply to Mr. Carmichael?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The minister had better "inspire" him. I do not advocate firing either Mr. Carmichael or Mr. Bell; both are high-class men. If Mr. Bell exceeded his instructions, he must have had a reason for doing it. I am not complaining especially about that statement of Mr. Bell; I am complaining about the effect created in the minds of the people of Canada who have still to be shaken out of their complacency with respect to winning this war. That, and nothing else, is the point of the reference.
I want to say this, and I have said it before, that we have done well in respect of the air training plan. It has been our biggest undertaking. I have often said that we started too late; but that is water over the dam; we have done well, and I want to give credit to the minister who fathered this scheme. He knows what I think about it. I have told him this on many occasions; and as far as I am concerned I do not want to embarrass for a minute either him or any other of the defence ministers; I want to help them.
I sometimes wonder whether the Canadian people will ever wake up to a knowledge of the life-and-death character of this struggle- and for us here in Canada. Sometimes I despair. Can it be that nothing but a blood bath, perhaps at our very doors, will awaken us to realities? Something has to be done to instil into the minds of the Canadian people -the danger which now confronts them.
The house will, I believe, bear with me a few moments while I make some references to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) of January 26. It will be recalled that near the outset of bis remarks he attempted, by banter and otherwise, to belittle the terms of the amendment which I had the honour to move. I confess that his observations left me cold. There is no one in this house who does not understand the purpose and the import of the amendment. Well, the words are there, "We shall be free to act and will act." What does that mean? If that is a sincere declaration-and I do not suggest that it is not-if released by the plebiscite, the government will then act to put the principle into effect. "Free to act and will act" means that the government will act affirmatively to put the principle into effect by repealing the limiting clause of the mobilization act. What other interpretation can any thoughtful person put upon that language? But compare that declaration with the language of the speech from the throne, and with that used by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister desired to be free to act, but never did he say that the government would act. On the contrary, the Prime Minister's declaration was a bid to the people to free him of his pledge and then allow him and his government to do as he pleased. Does the minister adhere to that, in the light of his declaration that the government when free to act, would act? The two positions are incompatible. No wonder the loyal people of this country are bewildered by the ambiguity of such a position and such declarations 1
I was glad, Mr. Speaker, to hear the minister address some plain and wholesome truths to . his supporters from the province of Quebec, and, above all, his challenge to their contention that under no circumstances should this nation compel its nationals to undertake military service abroad. What he said needed to be said. Why? Because for twenty-five years the people of Quebec have been taught in season and out of season, by the leaders of the Liberal party in that province and, indeed, by others high in the councils of that party, that they had no national obligation to the state, to the empire, to the world at large in such circumstances as have now developed. He did well to remind our French-Canadian compatriots that this struggle was not one for imperial aggrandizement but a life-and-death conflict between two philosophies of life, between freedom and slavery; and that this struggle will be decided not within the territorial limits of Canada but in theatres of war far distant from our shores. Indeed he might and should have gone much further and pointed out to them that their ideas of
imperialism, which have been so repugnant to them, are ideas which are outmoded and no longer in existence. In this twentieth century, Mr. Speaker, imperialism means trusteeship, not aggrandizement. That is a principle which the minister might very well have brought home to his compatriots, but he missed the golden opportunity.
But on the principle of cabinet responsibility and solidarity the minister backed up and endeavoured to justify the plebiscite, and he announced his intention of supporting it in the country. Having taken a noble stand in the early part of his address, he boxed the whole compass. He started off with the lofty attitude of a statesman; he took his seat with the stature of a party politician.
I want now to put this question squarely to him: If the testing time comes, will he support the principle of compulsory military service? And will the government act? He should make his position clear. The people of Canada want to know. The people of Nova Scotia want to know. They will not be content with a declaration of "wait and see." That policy smacks of opportunism, of putting party politics above the safety of the state, and that is not good enough. The manly course is to say and say now what the government will do if the plebiscite carries. And if the plebiscite fails to carry, what then will the minister do? Will he say, "I bow to the will of the majority no matter if I disagree on a great matter of principle"? If I apprehend the minister's position aright, as disclosed by his speech, he will resign; and he will be right, and his people will applaud him. If the result is indecisive, and if eight provinces out of nine vote "yes" and one great province votes "no", as well it may; what then? Will he adopt one of the only two courses open to him, that of resigning on a matter of principle, or will he proceed on the British principle of constitutional government, which as a student of the law and of the constitution he must believe in, namely, the adoption of a policy on this question, one way or the other, and stake his political life on the position he then takes?
May I commend to him and to this house the authority of a great student and writei on the law of the constitution. Dicey, where in chapter 94 he discusses and sums up the argument against introducing the principle of the plebiscite into parliamentary institutions, and where he advocates the doctrine of the rule of intelligence. The late Lord Asquith was a great lawyer, a great parliamentarian, a great orator and a great debater; someone has said he was the last of the great Liberals. I think I should qualify that and designate the

I want now to say a word about the loan; and I suspect that the minister made his speech when he did, and said some of the things he did say, not so much in support of a bad case for the plebiscite but because he was alarmed for the success of the loan, and he had reason for that fear. When I first read of the plebiscite proposal, one of my first reactions was that the proposal, put forward in the form it -was and at the time it was, would be disastrous. The timing was frightful, having regard to the loan. The minister has been hearing from the country, and so have I. The minister made a vigorous attack upon some of those who wrote him. He called them saboteurs of the national war effort, and declared that their action was a strike against the state.
I do not think that calling names will help his position. Rather would I commend to him the appeal to reason when dealing with these people. Apparently a large number of people have been writing the minister, threatening to cancel their pledges to buy war savings certificates, and to boycott the victory loan, as a means of expressing their disapproval of the government's subterfuge of a plebiscite on an important issue.
Human nature being what it is, that is a natural thing for some people to do. I have heard it on many sides. But I deprecate that attitude; I oppose it. On cool reflection I am sure those who have so declared, themselves will reverse their judgment.
Let me make my position and the position of the Conservative party clear on this issue. Notwithstanding our disapproval of the government's policy, notwithstanding our belief that it is a policy of evasion of responsibility, and the negation of responsible government, we believe that the loan should and must be supported to the limit, and I appeal here and now to the great army of loyal Conservatives in this country, as well as to the great mass of our citizens, to rise above the situation which the government has created and which they abhor, and put this loan over.
To them I say: That is the nobler course; that is the patriotic course; that is the course which national obligation imposes; that is the

course which we owe to the men overseas and to those we are asking to go overseas to fight for us, to defend us. Any other course is unthinkable-any other course will but play into the hands of the isolationists, the unpatriotic, the disloyal. Let it never be said that this nation stultified itself. The wealth of the nation must be put at the disposal of the state. It must be marshalled and mobilized. Yes, and if needs be, if it means the winning of the war, it must be conscripted. Let there be no mistake on that score.
Many times I have told this house that the people of Canada would give the government the money to carry on the war, give it in abundance and in full measure. They will hold them accountable for how it is expended. That prophecy has been amply justified up to now. It will continue to be justified. I have supreme confidence that no matter how distasteful government policies may be, no matter how much we abhor the lack of leadership so apparent in this plebiscite, the loyal people of Canada, who all along have been ahead of the government in a determination to pursue total war with total effort, will never stultify themselves. I know they will not do it.
I endorse the minister's appeal in this regard. The great army of Conservatives in Canada will respond to the nation's need in full measure.
May I turn now to the amendment which I had the honour to move on January 26, and which is based on two fundamental principles. The first relates to the proposal for the plebiscite. I shall not take time at this point to read it.
I dealt with the question of the plebiscite at considerable length in my previous address, and I do not propose to repeat my arguments to-day.
I would, however, commend to the Prime Minister and to all thoughtful students of parliamentary government the .highly significant and reasoned address delivered to this house on Monday, the 9th instant, by the hon. member for Ontario. I regretted that the Prime Minister was not present to hear that speech. As a student, as a Liberal, he could not have listened to it without some heart-burnings and stirrings of mind and conscience; for the hon. member put the matter of plebiscite and government responsibility before this house and before the people of Canada far better than I am capable of doing, far better than anyone else so far has done. With inescapable logic, with apt phrase and sound reasoning, he exposed the fallacy of the government's proposal.

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
The second underlying principle of my amendment is my attempt to state, in general but unmistakable terms, the principles under which I think this country can and should wage war. I shall not read it, but it is a matter of record.
There is no ambiguity about this amendment. We propose the complete utilization of everything we possess to wage total war and to attain victory. It includes much more than the mere mobilization of our man-power for service anywhere. It visualizes the utmost use of our wealth and material resources to back up our man-power. It means among other things, the conscription of wealth, to accomplish that end. Indeed, we have the power to conscript wealth to-day. Up to date the power has been exercised in a very limited degree, but the power is there to be used and the people of this country are prepared to make this or any other sacrifice if called upon to do so. All they require is to be told what to do. I have scores of letters from men who are capable, willing and anxious to do something, but they do not know where to go to do it. Our people will never refuse this or any other government all the tools that are necessary, including, if needs be, both their lives and their wealth.
There is a great deal of mixed thinking on this question of conscription of wealth.
Taxation-heavy and severe taxation such as that to which we have subjected ourselves -is a form of conscription. The direct deduction of the national defence tax from the mechanic's pay cheque is a form of conscription. The levy of income tax is another form; but it is not confiscation, because any income tax is predicated on the theory that there must be capital and/or services upon which the income is earned and these are to be maintained; else there is nothing to tax. We have conscription in the form of the new Dominion Succession Duty Act.
Yes, let us completely mobilize the wealth of the country to attain total w*ar! But do not believe-and I direct the attention of hon. members to this point-that such mobilization means the complete nationalization of all our financial institutions, as my friends on the left pretend they would have us do. That is socialism, pure and unadulterated.
I reject socialism, because it not only eliminates the principle of private enterprise but contemplates a definite revolution in our economic fabric. Most of us are individualists. I believe we all pride ourselves upon being individualists. I am, and I admit it without shame or apology. But I do recognize that in war time I must subordinate my undoubted rights as an individual to the paramount necessities of the state-even, perhaps, under
the censorship to which we referred the other day. I may for a while not object to the viciousness of a censor. But I am not willing to give up my rights forever.
The official opposition finds it impossible to support the subamendment of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Let me analyse that amendment. In part it states that:
In the opinion of this house no total effort adequate to meet the present needs of the war, domestic problems, and the preparation for postwar conditions is possible without total mobilization of wealth, industry and finance as well as human resources.
The underlying thought of that section of the subamendment is much the same as that part of my amendment to be found in subparagraph (a) which reads:
(a) completely mobilize the wealth and material resources and, on a selective basis, the full man and woman power of the nation, to the end that the nation may wage total war in any theatre of war.
To that part of the subamendment I can not take exception. But if he so intended, he has not expressed it-

One form of socialism. That is what these gentlemen mean, and for myself I certainly cannot accept it. However, in voting against it we are not to be taken as disapproving "total mobilization of wealth, industry and finance as well as human resources."
The fourth part of my amendment refers to the question of post-war problems. One cannot, within the brief compass of a speech, touch upon all the topics with which one would desire to deal. I put that clause in my amendment because there is definitely no reference to this matter in the speech from the throne. If the Minister of Pensions and National Health will give me his attention, I should like to say that I referred to this in the amendment because I recall that in a speech which he delivered in Quebec city on June 20 last he painted a glowing picture of what was to be at the conclusion of peace-a peace, he

declared, dictated "by the people" and a postwar world where problems will be solved "by the will of the masses of the people." He then proceeded:
Never again, I hope and pray, shall you and I know the Canada we knew before this war broke upon us

when unemployment and relief and distress and hunger and poverty and want were rampant in the richest country in all the world. The new day, the new order, the new plan must bring, and will bring, a remedy for all that.
I can just hear him raising his voice to high heaven. He then went on to speak of a policy of collective security based upon collective force and collective preparedness rather than upon collective idealism. But he failed to sketch the new plan, like so many people who talk about the ideal condition that is to be when this war is over. It is true he gave his vision of post-war Canada, a vision of timed public works, of coordinated municipal, provincial and federal effort, of progressive highway development-nothing new about that; they have all been tried and they will not bring about the millennium-to be ruled by a sound and progressive agricultural policy. We are still waiting for that. He omitted to refer to the soundness of the principle of private enterprise. Has he divorced himself from that? Is he fearful of that?
Then, rising to great heights of eloquence- I can hear him now-he adopted the classic cry of the old London watch: "Watchmen, what of the night?" from the book of Isaiah. And he quoted the answer:
The night is far spent-the long, long night is nearly over-the morning cometh.
And he wound up with this prediction:
We shall soon witness the glory of the dawn.
Magnificent! My heart glowed when I read the report of that speech, but I fear we have not yet witnessed the glory of the dawn and we are not likely to until victory is won. Meanwhile, what of the preparations for the post-war period? In his speech of February 6 the minister stated that the government had submitted to the house a series of far-reaching measures dealing with post-war problems and announced that at least two further important measures would be submitted at the present session. He cited the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 as being primarily a post-war measure. I concur in a degree, but no one, even rising to the wildest heights of his imagination, can ever say that unemployment insurance is a cure for unemployment. It is merely a palliative.
He then referred to the post-discharge plan, passed somewhat belatedly, I believe, by means of an order in council, after he had been hearing from the returned soldiers and the

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
country. This gives the benefit of the Unemployment Insurance Act to members of the armed forces and provides certain other measures of assistance to discharged men, and the minister referred to it as a post-war measure of the highest importance. In a degree that is also true, but it, too, is merely a palliative and not a cure for what may be.
He then stated that of the measures to be introduced this session one would deal with a system of land settlement which would be one of the most constructive and far-reaching proposals of its kind ever submitted to parliament. We may expect something enormous. We shall reserve judgment with regard to this announcement, but I should like to say this to him and to members of the government: Be sure to benefit by the history of the past. I lay it down as axiomatic-it is no use putting a man on the land who does not have his roots deep in the soil and a love for the soil. Furthermore, any man put on the land should have had some knowledge of farming prior to his enlistment. Over and above all-as important as any at all events- before asking a man to go on the land the government of this country and the provincial governments should propose and put. into effect, by coordinated effort if possible, policies which will result in farmers receiving for their products such financial returns as will make it profitable for them to go on the land and remain there. This is fundamental, and if you do not do that, no land policy will succeed.
Most people in this country are and have been fearful that when the war is over and a lasting peace, let us hope, is attained, large numbers of our people will find themselves out of jobs and that we shall experience a depression far greater than that after the last war and greater even than that of the great depression period.
May I suggest that these prophets of calamity bear in mind that the biggest job on our hands apart from the war, and as big a job at least as that of defence, will be waiting for the people of Canada-the job of rebuilding our national economy-and that a depression need not occur unless by private and official folly one is created.
In this connection may I refer hon. members to a speech made by Mr. W. J. Cameron on the Ford Sunday Evening Hour on October 12 last, in which he deals with this matter and deals with it realistically. He said:
Look at the factors. First, a production plant largely obsolete for years, never able to supply all our people, is now being modernized and enlarged.	Second, a general stock so
greatly reduced by defence restrictions on manufacture and purchases that, with defence secured, the demand for all sorts of merchandise will require every man and machine we have to satisfy it.	Third, new industries like
aviation being firmly established, the use of plastics extended, older industries rejuvenated and a closer partnership formed between larger and smaller businesses. Fourth, with its production mechanism smashed to pieces, where can Europe look for the means of rehabilitation after the victory, except to America? Why, it will require twenty years of shipbuilding alone to replace the bottoms that have been sunk the last two years! These factors unless we are hopeless fools, will help to accomplish the transition without hard times.
Then he goes on to state that a depression was in the cards following previous wars, but that this time it is not in the cards, that conditions are different. Many minds are giving forethought to preventing a depression, but nothing can protect us or our nation against ourselves. Then he adds this wholesome admonition and preaches the doctrine of thrift which I should like to have every man, woman and child in Canada take to heart:
Let those who are earning more money put some of it where they can get it back. A spending panic is as bad as a hoarding panic. We can protect our nation and we can protect ourselves if we assert and believe, on the basis of facts, that a post-defence depression is not necessary and can be avoided.
I apologize, Mr. Speaker, for having spoken so long, but perhaps the house will bear with me for about five minutes more.
To me the plebiscite is as objectionable as when it was first announced. But the government will not alter its course. It will pass the address notwithstanding the opposition which comes from various diverse elements, and for various reasons. That being so, we should next await the government's proposals with respect to the modus operandi of the plebiscite. Let us examine them judicially with a view, if possible, to improving them. During this debate we have not had much light thrown on this topic-the discussion has centred around the principles involved. Let us then turn our attention to the proposals, and examine them as business men, not as partisans. I shall then, I hope, have crystallized my views on what I think I should advise our people to do.
Then we can turn to the general business of the session. I have offered the government, and I renew this offer, constructive cooperation in its general war programme. I have tried to follow a consistent course in that regard, no matter what certain critics have said, and I shall continue to do so. I may not be a Willkie, but no one will ever be able to say that I and those who sit round me have sabotaged or obstructed the government's war effort. On the contrary, we have sought and shall seek to help the government by constructive criticism, but we must not be ex-

The Address-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
pected to submerge our opinions on matters of principle. That we shall never do. That we should not be expected to do.
I listened on Sunday, as all hon. gentlemen no doubt did, to Mr. Churchill's speech in which near the close he announced the fall of Singapore. I listened to it with mingled feelings. Here was disaster; here was defeat. But I was buoyed up with his soul-stirring message to us and the other nations, and I shall close by quoting one paragraph from his address which sank into my heart, my mind and my soul. He said:
This, therefore, is one of those moments when the British nation can show its quality of genius. This is one of those moments when it can draw from the heart of misfortune the vital impulse of victory. Here is a moment to display that calm and poise, combined with grim determination, which not so very long ago brought us out of the very jaws of death. Here is another occasion to show, as so often in our long history, that we can meet reverses with dignity and with renewed accession of strength.

speechtext:
The question is on the amendment.	

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-*couata): Mr. Speaker, I have not spoken on the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition and I intend to say a few words.
It seems to me it is important to give the house an idea of the real feeling and sentiment of the province of Quebec. Members who live one-half of the year in their constituencies have one superiority over those who have not the same advantage on account of pressure of business. They meet thirty, forty, fifty people each weekday-people who tell them about their joys and their troubles and ask them for information and help. Of course all those who come to the office of a member do not give information about personal matters. Some come just to ask for a recommendation, or a word of encouragement. But others have sufficient confidence in their member of parliament to tell him about very personal matters, to open up their hearts to him and ask for advice. They also inform the member about the general feeling of those who live near them and of the community in which they reside. Therefore a member of parliament has the advantage of knowing well the feeling and sentiment of his constituents. So that when the opinion of members of parliament is asked by the government, it is very easy for them to inform the government about the soundness or unsoundness of any policy.
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, hon. members exchange gibes in this house. They try to break the monotony and dullness of the proceedings with some repartee; but though this happens at times I must congratulate very heartily and very warmly not only the mover and seconder of the address but all my colleagues who have taken part in this debate, from the Prime Minister down. We realize the seriousness of the moment, but what I cannot comprehend is the use of commonplace sayings when each of us should be at liberty to speak with more freedom than ever in expressing his own views. Whether or not my colleagues share my views, there is one thing I must and will do; that is, respect their views.
With the loss of our mutual friend, the late Minister of Justice, this House of Commons reminds me of the Quebec seminary where I was a student, after one of the greatest educators in Canada, Monsignor Mathieu, had left that institution to become the first archbishop of Regina. At times I have seen the broad smile of the former Minister of Justice, even while I was speaking; and once I remember he told me he had been told by someone sitting in front of him not to smile when I was speaking, because he was encouraging me. As I rise to speak to-day, sir, I
remember some events of my political life, particularly the day when the former Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, came with my leader, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the house in which I live, at Riviere du Loup. Though notice of this event had been given only a short time before, and the weather was bad, some eight hundred people from my county came in to pay their tribute of respect both to my leader, the leader of the Liberal party, who was then leader of the opposition, and to their old friend the Minister of Justice. The Prime Minister, I am sure, must remember the kind faces of those good people. Many of them were farmers; and they all said how delighted they were to have the privilege oL shaking hands with him. Among them was an old gentleman who died a year or two ago at the age of ninety-four, who had voted for my grandfather, for my father, and for myself, and who used to preside at my meetings. He was a dear old gentleman, tall and with a long white beard; and I introduced him to my leader as the Liberal patriarch of my county. The Prime Minister was thoughtful enough to send that old gentleman birthday messages of greetings and good wishes each year until his unfortunate death.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this is not an exceptional case. I am proud of my people. I respect them. When I speak to them, and when they do me the honour of listening to my speeches, I consider it a very great privilege. It is a great sacrifice for me to remain in politics. I could have an easy life otherwise, but it is my duty in time of war to stand by my people and show my appreciation of the confidence they have placed in me during the long time I have represented them in this House of Commons.
This afternoon I listened to the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson)-I wonder if he is still acting, or if he is the full leader? He said, "If we do not face realities we may lose this war." I agree with that. Then he added, "We, the loyal people, are bewildered." It sounded like, "We, the people of England; the 'tailors of Tooley street.' " Is he the only person in Canada who is not complacent? Speaking of the plebiscite he said it was neither the manly nor the courageous course, and then he spoke of the probability of the invasion of England. The question is not whether the plebiscite is a manly or courageous course. The question is whether the plebiscite is the best course to follow at the present time, bearing in mind also that the plebiscite is closely related to conscription for overseas service. Then the hon. gentleman said the province of Quebec
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

should understand that this war is a conflict between two philosophies of life, freedom and slavery. A friend of mine who occupies a high post in the government of Quebec told me once that French-Canadians are not strong for abstraction. There is one point however I should like now to suggest to the government. I have already made the suggestion, but unfortunately it was not accepted. I suggest that a radical change be made in the information service of the government.
Why do we have trouble and agitation on the part of people in Toronto and elsewhere who have advocated total war? We have it because the information service of the government is totally inefficient, and because it is headed by a man who has been loaned by a big company and who receives at least SI 5 a day for expenses, while at the same time receiving salary. He is a neurasthenic and a fascist. How can fascist propaganda be dear to the hearts of French-Canadians in Quebec, any more than to the hearts of the good English-speaking or French-speaking citizens in other parts of Canada? This I do not understand. There should be a radical change in that regard. Moreover, with regard to information, the province of Quebec should be given the same brain food as any other part of Canada. We are all citizens of the same country, and I cannot understand why one story should be told in Quebec and another in Ontario, the maritimes and the west.
There is one other point I have stated before; let me repeat it. The day when our English-speaking oompatriots will have with regard to Great Britain the same views we French-Canadians have toward France. That day we shall have a perfect union of hearts in Canada. As we are at war it is essential to have enough courage to take the necessary steps to bring about a most efficient war effort. What do I mean when I say that? I mean that each one should be at his place, so that he can do the best possible to help the country win the war.
There are farmers' sons who would like to enlist but who cannot. They are in the same position as any young man who has a beautiful and charming sweetheart he cannot marry now because he has to take care of his old parents. That applies to many farmers' sons. Although my offer to recruit a whole regiment in my constituency was turned down two years ago, yet from the city of Riviere du Loup, with a population of only 9,000, over 1,200 boys have enlisted in the three branches of the service. From Cabano, a town in my constituency with a population of
2,000,	over 250 boys have enlisted voluntarily in the army.

Very often farmers are confronted with the problem of choosing between entering the army and putting a padlock on the old homestead or the old farm which for generations has been cultivated by the same family. Everyone knows that Great Britain can live only with the supplies shipped from all parts of the world. What the farmers are doing for this country-and when I refer to this country I include the army as well as the civilian population-they are doing for Great Britain. They are doing the same even for Russia, since the invasion of the fertile plains of the Ukraine by the barbarous huns.
Our friend Mr. Lapointe, the former Minister of Justice, lived in my constituency for many years. He was born there, and he loved it so much that even last summer he paid it a visit, as he had done each year, to spend some months of relaxation. In August, 1940, after the National Resources Mobilization Act was passed, he had been working very strenuously in Ottawa, and proceeded to Temiscouata county to take a vacation. While he was away from Ottawa, regulations were drafted in virtue of the mobilization act, and according to those regulations farming as well as other essential occupations were classed as seasonal. Mr. Lapointe was not here when those regulations were approved by order in council. They were drafted by men who knew no more about agriculture than the fellow who sees a horse and then says, "What a nice cow!" or sees a cow and says, "What a fine colt.!" They knew positively nothing about agriculture.
What happened afterward? Members of parliament had to carry on the fight with the authorities to have opportunity given farmers to stay on the land and continue their work -a work which is not "secondary", but which is essential.
Listening to speeches in the house and reading them in Hansard I have been pleased to note that even hon. members favouring the conscription of man-power have suggested the exemption of farmers on the very ground that their work is essential to Canada in a time of war as well as in a time of peace. May I pay tribute to the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson); to his very able deputy, General LaFleche; to General LaFleche's associate, Major Benoit; to the registrar at Quebec city and his staff, and, now that some improvement has been made in the commission of our district, to the commission itself.
Members of parliament are deluged with requests, and they are reasonable requests, from farmers for delay in their training. I am ready to do any useful work for my constitu-

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
ents even if I have to work day and night. I am ready to argue the case of the farmers in my constituency with any official in the Department of National War Services or the Department of National Defence. But this is a ridiculous burden to be placed upon members of parliament; these cases should be taken care of automatically. As soon as the man can show that he is farming in earnest, that he is able to do his work well as a farmer, that he is contributing to feeding the army and the civilians of this country, he should be permitted to continue to do his work without being disturbed.
I should like to read a few remarks made by my leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), on June 19, 1940, as reported on page 922 of Hansard. He said:
An hon. member on this side of the house made the statement publicly this morning that he felt he could go into his constituency and, by making it known to his constituents that this measure had to do with the protection of Canada and our own Canadian soil, bring forward in a very short time men from the forests, from the fields and from the factories, all prepared immediately [DOT] to join the Canadian forces to resist any possible invasion, and that he would be prepared to guarantee that that could be done in constituency after constituency throughout the country, once it was understood that there was the necessity of defending our own Canadian shores. I pointed out to him that in doing that he might be making the greatest mistake possible with respect to the national interest; that, to win this war, we might wish to keep at work in the forests the men who are now working in the forests, to provide the timber which will be required for docks and wharves and required immediately; that the men who are working in the factories may be a thousand times more useful to the government of this country in giving their skilled labour to the manufacture of aircraft, munitions, or other weapons of war than they could possibly be in lining up and presenting themselves for military service; equally- that on the farms, if we are to perform what will be expected of us, we shall need all the production that can be effectively and rapidly carried out on the farms of our country.
That was expressed much better than I could say it. I urge hon. members to read this in Hansard to-morrow. I do not find it absurd to have to come to the assistance of farmers, farmers' sons and farmers' helpers. What I find absurd is to have to do this work, sometimes without satisfactory results, when the matter could be definitely and automatically settled. These farmers should be allowed to continue to do their work in peace until the war is over, and even afterwards. Our farmers, settlers and farm hands are the most stable element we have in this country. Moreover they are the ones who have time to think and to think right. No government in this country can expect to serve us, no party
can expect to serve us, unless they keep faith with our farmers.
Why did the Conservative party headed by Sir Robert Borden lose the confidence of the Canadian people? Because they broke the pledge they gave to the farmers that conscription would never be imposed upon them. When the farmers came to Ottawa they found that the doors were shut against them. They were not received then any more than they were received afterwards when Mr. Bennett was Prime Minister and had the Royal Canadian Mounted Police with loaded guns waiting to receive such peaceful people as the farmers of our country.
I do not want the Liberal party to fall into the ditch where the Tory party has been stagnant since the last war. I sincerely believe that the Liberal party is the only force that can maintain order when this war is over and after we have won it.
We were told the other day by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) that in the province of Quebec we did not understand the meaning of a total war effort. My fellow citizens of the province of Quebec understand quite well what is a total war effort. They apply to this -country the well known proverb that charity begins at home. They want to s*e this country well protected in the east as well as in the west and in the centre. They are good Canadians and they understand that their duty is to defend the shores of British Columbia as well as the shores of the maritime provinces and their own. They are ready to do anything they can to help Great Britain win this war, and the proof of this is the number of French-Canadians who have enlisted from my part of the country. But they want this country to be well defended. Before any move is made to impose conscription for overseas service they want the defence of this country to be complete and assured.
After consultation with some of our colleagues, it is my duty as the private Liberal member for Temiseouata to move, seconded bv my hon. colleague and friend the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lizotte), the following amendment to the amendment:
That all the words after the words "this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers", in the said amendment be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
are contemplating, with regard to conscription of man-power for overseas service, a reversal of policy yvhich is uncalled for, untimely and detrimental to the defence of Canada;
I should like the farmers of York-Sunbury to see the grin on the face of their member at this moment. Not one of them surely would vote for him if they had seen him this after-
The Address-Mr. Lacombe

noon grinning as I spoke of the distress of the farmers. I continue the reading of my amendment:
This house further holds the view that the defence of Canada should always have priority over any commitment with or in favour of any other country and also that it would be in the. interest of Canada and our allied countries as well that farmers and farm hands should be exempted from the military service.
I regret, sir, that the only way open to me to carry out what I propose is to move a subamendment. I do know that some officials of some of the departments hold the same opinions as I and many other members have, regarding the necessity of exempting farmers and farm hands from military service because their work is really a war work. But on account of the stupidity of so-called experts this has not yet been decided upon. That is to be regretted. For the common good it should be made easier for the farmers to continue with their work in peace. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but with so many countries at war and out of production it is all the more necessary for us to stop this policy of cutting the acreage under production, and instead, to get more and more farm goods produced. We do not know what will happen after the war, but certainly it will take time for many warring countries to recuperate and produce enough even for their own consumption. Therefore I urge the government to appreciate that what is being done now by the mover and the seconder of this amendment is not anything that is detrimental to the Liberal party or to the welfare of this country, but rather it is something that should have been done two years ago when we declared war. At that time it was mentioned vaguely, and I congratulate the government upon having changed the regulations of the national war services department to provide, by order in council, that farming is an essential as well as a seasonal occupation. But that is not enough. It was a mistake to state in those regulations that farming was a secondary occupation. It is not. The farmers have to work from dawn to dusk in winter as well as in summer. I urge the government to strike out the word "secondary," leaving in the word, "essential." I earnestly hope that the government will accept the subamendment as their policy with regard to the farmers of this country.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment which the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has just moved to the amendment has my unqualified support. I will vote for it with satisfaction, knowing that I shall be performing a great duty towards agriculture. The agricultural industry is and re-

mains our first line of defence. We should ensure the defence of Canada first of all by protecting our farmers through exemption from military training and from compulsory military service.
The hon. member for Temiscouata need have no regrets. He is moving in the right direction, and I follow him with pleasure on the path of Canadianism and of honour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must protest against ithe amendment just proposed by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and seconded by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lizotte). I do not know what the people of the old country can be thinking of us and of Canada at the present time. If it were not for the glorious British army, navy and air force, that slumbereth not nor sleepeth while Canada talks, the enemy would have descended upon the St. Lawrence before this and blown down the citadel at Quebec.
May I say to my hon. friend the member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), who wants to change the flag, that he had better hang on to the union jack because if Hitler comes over here-and the enemy is not far from our shores at this moment-it will be the black flag that will be hung on the citadel at Quebec and on the parliament buildings at Ottawa-and there will not be any referendum about that either. I protest against this amendment. The city of Toronto sent 55,000 men to the last war, 4,700 of whom lie buried in France until the resurrection morning. They fought for Canada, Britain and the glorious country of France, which in the last war did so much to ensure that freedom and liberty and civilization shall not perish from the earth. Let me say to my hon. friends from the province of Quebec- and I have a great many friends amongst them-what I said when I first entered this house, that no city in the world is less bigoted than the city of Toronto from which I come. Nowhere do protestants and catholics and all races and classes of our people get on better together than they do in Toronto. Toronto subscribed one-third to the victory loan and enrolled of its citizens who enlisted from there and in other cities across Canada nearly one-third of the recruits for the army, navy and air force. They did not need to be conscripted. They did not need to be sent to the war because our young people rose as one man to serve, and if we had had a proper system of recruiting in this country we would have had a million men now under arms under the voluntary system, although the other system is fairer and more equitable to all.

The Address-Mr. Church
I object to the principle of this amendment. Farmers' sons in our province in the last war did not want to be exempted. The farmers of Ontario showed their patriotism in going to the war, and they were patriots at the ballot box on election day when they asserted the rights and privileges of the people of Ontario in respect of the reciprocity treaty of 1911-that much-attacked province which is contributing more men, money and munitions than any of the other provinces.
The enemy is not far from our shores at the present time. But for the British fleet and air force, Quebec, the maritimes and Ontario would long ago have had first-hand experience of the concentration camp, the loud-speaker, the sergeant-major, the spy, the tramping of feet, the gestapo, the whip, the spirit of barbarism, brutality and savagery. I repeat that but for Britain we should have known these things long ago in Canada from coast to coast; yet we sit here day in and day out, debating such things as this amendment, refusing to pay a tribute to the people of the mother country who are bearing the brunt of the war and, up to the last summer, were bearing it alone over the whole civilized world, fighting our battles on the Atlantic, in the Mediterranean, in Libya and every other place. There is no such thing as home defence as applied to Quebec, or Three Rivers, or Montreal, or Ottawa, or Winnipeg, which can have any bearing on our future. The defence of Canada will not be at those cities; it will be decided in Europe and Asia. There is, indeed, no such thing as home defence in modern warfare. We must go wherever the enemy is. The fate of civilization for the next two hundred years is being decided on the shores of Britain, in Russia, in the Mediterranean, on the sands of Libya, and in the Pacific-that great ocean which is lost to us to-day, in which Japan is dominant in sea power-and the fate of freedom is in the scales. Talk about building a road to Alaska; all the bases which may be belatedly constructed at the Pacific coast will not count a snap of the fingers without sea power to back them up on the Pacific, because without control of the sea you cannot transport either troops or food or munitions or anything else to the endangered areas in the Pacific without a base. If the battle of the Atlantic is lost, the same consequences will follow.
For over two years of the war Britain had to fight and go it alone. Later we found two new allies-Russia and the United States. The latter country was not ready for war; like Canada, she had been listening to the babble of the pacifists and isolationists. Canada urged Britain to throw away her army, navy
and air force, and did the same herself, with the result that when war came we were not prepared. We threw away our defences and our friends.
All this talk about home defence and the plebiscite which the hon. member for Temis-couata mentions in his amendment is just a smoke-screen gotten up and thrown out at the last moment to cover up the mistakes some of whose consequences we have seen in the Pacific-Singapore, Hong Kong and other places. As I understand the hon. member's amendment, he wants to exempt farmers' sons and railway employees. They are not asking to be exempted. I have spoken of one province where the farmers are going to the war. The hon. member stated that a plebiscite is a reversal of policy. There I agree with him. It is true. Did you ever know this government to carry out any of their pledges, either as regards trade, defence, immigration, armaments, or anything else? I never have. They had posters on the billboards, "Beat Bennett and Bad Times". Well, they beat Bennett but they did not beat bad times. "End Unemployment; Vote Liberal". The people voted Liberal but the government did not end unemployment. So much for their pledges to get in on, but never to stand on. If there is a reversal of policy, it is just an afterthought at the last minute to tide things over until such time as the situation rights itself, and to save the wrath of the people.
What are the people of eastern Canada depending upon for their defence? Are these hon. members representative or typical of opinion in Quebec and Ontario? I admit that these two provinces have done very well, but the enemy would have been here long ago- in the spring of 1940 they would have come up the St. Lawrence by air and sea, but for that one agency, the mother country, which has protected our shores in peace and war alike, ever since we have been a country.
I concede that the hon. member who moved this amendment possesses some likable qualities. Sometimes he speaks out, like the former house leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) on behalf of the underdog and the common people; sometimes, I think, he goes too far at times about Conservatives, and in this motion to exempt the sons of farmers, and railway workers, he has gone too far. Nor do I agree with him in his plea about home defence. I can tell him this, and the government likewise, that there is no such thing as home defence. We found that out on the Pacific coast. We threw overboard our old ally, Japan, which had been a good friend to us and to the empire; we threw Italy over-
The Address-Mr. Church

board; we supposed that we could discard our own defences and our friends as well-with the results which are now evident in the Pacific. The situation is very grave at present for the people of our great Pacific province, and it is not going to be cured by the sort of home defence which is indicated in this amendment, or by holding secret meetings of this house which will cover up our mistakes. As I said yesterday, secret meetings about what? About home defence? About nothing. There is nothing to hold a meeting about. The British people in their own house, as is evidenced in ninety-five pages of Hansard published last January, have gone into the whole trouble at Singapore, Hong Kong and other points in the Pacific.
Our people are getting sick of this talk of home defence and plebiscite. Canada is being injured in the eyes of our empire. Last session I asked the minister to produce papers on the subject of home defence for cities, and he replied that it was a matter for the localities interested. They might lend them a few magic-lanterns and some sirens and whistles to blow, or fireworks, but as for providing an army, navy or air force, there is not a thing for home defence in any city in Ontario, excepting the black-out. There is no use in fooling the people into supposing they are secured by measures of this kind or any other provision for local defence which is simply no home defence at all. Home defence simply and mostly consists of one local volunteer company, the police, the girl guides and the boy scouts, and it can be nothing else, even though the people of the good county of Temiscouata should send five or six members to the House of Commons. All Canada is dependent on the mother country to defend us.
There is no doubt that the plebiscite is a reversal of policy, not mentioned in the 1940 election. Even lion, members who support the government knew nothing about it until the proposal was introduced to the house. Did you ever hear of such a thing? The people of this country know that, in the first year of the war, without a plebiscite, mechanized hordes swept over Norway, Czechoslovakia, the low countries,-Belgium, Holland, Denmark-France and all Europe, all of which countries had been talking about home defence One of the countries which was overrun, Luxembourg, had a police force of 250. In the second year of the war the enemy conquered Jugoslavia and Greece. Their "home defence" fell to the ground and amounted to nothing. I can tell you this: but for the agency I have named, Britain, the enemy would long ago have been in the

maritimes, in the province of Quebec, and through Ontario right to the head of the lakes.
I did not intend to speak in this debate, but I object to the remarks which have been made about the soldier city of Toronto. We are not sitting up all night long worrying about Quebec. I know the people of Toronto; I was born there. They are hard-working patriotic citizens. I have never had any bigotry in me, nor have I ever met a bigoted citizen there, and I am only one of five or six hundred thousand persons similarly conditioned. We are not worrying about Quebec or any other province; our only worry is to win the war. We like the people of Quebec; they are our own kith and kin; they have done a great deal for Canada, and in this war they have done better than they did in the last-the records speak for themselves. But let me say that I hope that in the speeches in this house we have heard the last of home defence and shall hear more of what we owe to the mother country, which has protected our shores and ourselves from the same air forces and mechanized hordes which overran the small countries of Europe, and threatened the very life of freedom and civilization.
